newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Foreign buyouts seen menacing Israel food sector.
newsitem.headline: Foreign buyouts seen menacing Israel food sector.

text.p: The string of acquisitions of Israeli food companies by multinational giants could cause a hollowing out of the local industry, a senior official from the Manufacturers Association warned on Tuesday.

"Thirty five percent of large factors in the industry (employing over 300 workers) have signed some sort of strategic agreement with a multinational in the past two to three years," Abraham Ben-Moshe, chairman of the association's food division, told reporters.
In addition, the Israeli government's import liberalisation programme was opening up the food sector to foreign competition without any benefit in return, he said.
Ben-Moshe said the new foreign owners might eventually decide to transfer production outside the country and leave their Israeli companies as distributors.

"In the case of CPC International most of the manufacturing is being done in Israel," Ben-Moshe said. "But there is another option: Some of the multinationals may decide to stop production here and will have purchased Israeli companies just to have a ready-made market."

CPC acquired a 24.5 percent stake in Israel Edible Products in February, increasing its holding to 75 percent. In addition, Danone has acquired a 20 percent stake in Strauss Dairies; Unilever PLC 50 percent of Strauss' ice cream business; and Nestle SA 40 percent of Osem Investments.
Ben-Moshe, who also serves as managing director of the Carmel wine cooperative, said the agreements were worth altogether about $300 million.

He said the buyouts had been encouraged by Israeli companies, which saw large foreign partners as a way of increasing their know-how and marketing power and protecting themselves in an increasingly competitive industry.
The acquisitions make it harder for smaller, independent firms to complete.

Liora Birnhack-Marcus, export manager for Manamim, said the $8 million-a-year family-owned confectionery maker had just invested $2 million in new equipment to compete with Nestle and other imported products.
"Either we do this or we disappear," she said.
Ben-Moshe said the multinational acquisitions were part of a worldwide trend towards increased concentration in the consumer products sector.

He said the Israeli industry's slowdown had not abated this year and predicted that its foreign trade deficit would grow to $290 million from $217 million in 1996. The Manufacturers Association expects exports to edge up only $2 million from last year to $610 million, while imports would grow nine percent to $900 million.
The industry's total sales would grow eight percent to $10.3 billion but in shekel terms sales they were barely keeping pace with inflation, Ben-Moshe said.
Investment in imported equipment would grow six percent in 1997 to $185 million.
"There is a growing phenomenon that is hurting the industry: Imports are growing at the expense of exports," Ben-Moshe said. "This is a result of government policy."
He said Israel's import-liberalisation programme had thrown open the country's food market to imports from Eastern Europe even though Israel did not enjoy reciprical terms.
For example, Israeli chocolate exports to Poland were subject to a 45 percent duty while Polish exports to Israel were duty-free.
Ben-Moshe said Israel's unilateral liberalisation programme had stripped it of any bargaining power when negotiating free trade area agreements.
